cells.tense: Right now you can feel what's owed here, and it is not up for debate.
cells.ask: Before you close out one loose end, say what's fair, then let the rest go. Keep the two minutes.
cells.core:
You can feel what's fair and you aren't arguing with yourself about it. Most people get a settled sense of what's owed and then talk themselves in circles; you go straight from feeling it to acting on it. That happens in small moments you don't notice.

What's finished can sit finished. Letting go isn't a loss you balance; it just frees the space. Before you close out one loose end, say what's fair, then let the rest go. Keep the two minutes. Fairness comes through clean when you aren't forcing it, and clean is what keeps it accurate rather than loud.
cells.sheetLine: You can feel what's fair and you don't argue about it.
cells.place: Where you let go of what's finished.

cells.tense: You are already rehearsing what next month should look like before this one has finished.
cells.ask: When a settlement with someone comes up and they haven't asked for one, put your answer down for a day and return to it. Name which side you're on.
cells.core:
Your sense of fairness runs heavier and faster than anyone asked for. You take a future moment — how a conversation ought to land, what someone will owe then — and furrow the ground before it's here. The compass is turned inward and magnetized, and it keeps pointing at the worst outcome unless you tip it outward again. That's what the heaviness is doing: solving for a score you can't yet see.

Use the strength that's already yours and hold it looser. When a settlement with someone comes up and they haven't asked for one, put your answer down for a day and return to it, not sooner. Name which side you're on — your own, or the fairness you can actually feel. The answer that arrives slower is the one you can trust.
cells.sheetLine: You're holding the future to a standard it hasn't met yet.
cells.place: Where you let go of what's finished.

cells.tense: You're still standing at a door where you agreed to something you didn't feel.
cells.ask: Once today, when something's asked of you, say what you actually feel about it before agreeing. Just the feeling, no story, and let that be enough.
cells.core:
The sense of fairness is still in you, but it's gone quiet. You agree at the right moments without hearing whether you meant it, and the checking has stopped on your side. Nothing is wrong with the instrument. It's that you're not giving it anywhere to land, so it stays folded up.

Build the practice rather than pushing the feeling. Once today, when something's asked of you, say what you actually feel about it before agreeing. Just the feeling, no story, and let that be enough. It comes back through the doing, not through the wishing. One honest answer is the whole exercise.
cells.sheetLine: You can feel what's fair. You just stopped bringing it home.

cells.tense: You are writing down what's fair in a room where you already left the pen.
cells.ask: Write one line today about something you know is right even when it costs you, then leave it and see if it holds.
cells.core:
You're already working out what's fair — weighing what was spilled against what still stands, in private, without announcing it. But you tell it as if the answers came from somewhere else: from the situation, from them, from what any reasonable person would say. The certainty is real. Claiming it isn't. So the careful work stays quiet, and the quiet makes it easy to think there's nothing there.

Write one line today about something you know is right even when it costs you. No explaining. Watch what your own certainty does before you check whether anyone agrees. That's how you learn whose voice it was.
cells.sheetLine: The fairness runs quiet because you haven't claimed it.
cells.place: Where you let go of what's finished.
